subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 58-year-old man is being screened for diabetes. A fasting blood sample is collected into a gray-top tube containing sodium fluoride so that the measured glucose will not fall while the sample is transported to the laboratory, and the reported fasting glucose is 126 mg/dL. A medical student asks how sodium fluoride preserves the glucose concentration in the sample.
question: Sodium fluoride prevents in vitro glucose consumption by inhibiting which of the following glycolytic enzymes?
explanation_correct: Sodium fluoride chelates magnesium and inhibits enolase, which converts 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate. Blocking this step stops glycolysis in leukocytes and erythrocytes, preventing the 5% to 7% per hour fall in glucose that otherwise occurs in an unprocessed blood sample; fluoride also inhibits several other glycolytic enzymes, but enolase is the classic target.

explanation_incorrect.B: Hexokinase catalyzes the first step of glycolysis and is feedback-inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate; it is not the enzyme blocked by fluoride.
explanation_incorrect.C: Phosphofructokinase-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis and is allosterically regulated by AMP, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, ATP, and citrate, not by fluoride.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final substrate-level phosphorylation of glycolysis and is not inhibited by fluoride.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase catalyzes the NAD+-dependent step of glycolysis and is not blocked by fluoride.

educationalObjective: Sodium fluoride preserves blood glucose by inhibiting enolase and thereby halting glycolysis in the sample.
